Academic Editor: Domenico Gabriele

Soy Protein Isolate (SPI), a widely sourced and versatile protein, is known for its high
protein concentration, rich amino acid profile, low saturated fat and substitutability. It
offers substantial benefits in the food, health, pharmaceutical and cosmetics industries
because of its functional qualities, which include gelation, emulsification and foaming [1].
Three-dimensional network structure, one of the significant advantages of the gel properties
of SPI, provides an excellent performance in several applications [2]. Its gelation property
can be used to enhance the texture, stability and storage properties of products. In the
manufacture of vegetarian and alternative meat products, soy isolate protein gels can
mimic meat and provide a high-quality source of protein. In addition, soy protein gel
is widely applied as pasta additives, beverages and nutraceuticals that aim at providing
its versatility in different manufacturing processes [3]. However, due to the limitation
of structure, the traditional heat-induced gelation method has deficiencies in increasing
gel strength, water retention ability and other factors, which cannot meet the production
requirements. To solve this problem, enzymes or ionic reagents, such as TGase or Ca2+,
are often used to induce SPI gels, which are able to initiate modification reactions under
relatively mild conditions to achieve improved protein functionality. TGase catalyzes the

and comprehensive network, contributing to enhance gel strength and stability [4]. As
it is temperature-independent of TGase-induced amide formation, it provides a greater
flexibility in gel formation under milder conditions [5]. Meanwhile, maintaining the
natural structure and functionality of SPI is particularly important in applications such as
substituting animal proteins, enhancing the nutritional value of foods by increasing the
protein content, such as in cereal bars, energy bars, or pH-sensitive food formulations.

Ultrasound technology, being a non-isothermal processing method, finds extensive use
in the realm of food processing, especially in modifying the physicochemical characteristics
of various food components [6,7]. It is extensively used in the soy protein modification
process, offering an efficient and controllable means of protein alteration due to harnessing
high-frequency sound waves. In the context of soy protein modification, ultrasonic treat-
ment enhances solubility by inducing conformational changes at the molecular level. It
also influences the physical and chemical structure of soy proteins, affecting secondary and
tertiary structures. According to Hu et al. [3], ultrasonication increases the solubility of SPI
dispersions by promoting the partial unfolding of SPI molecules. It increases the amount
of free sulfhydryl (SH) and surface hydrophobicity (H0), while decreasing particle size.
Khatkar et al. [8] discovered that ultrasonic treatment improved the hydration, thermal
properties and in vitro protein digestibility of soy protein. Ultrasound can promote the
increased exposure of active groups, facilitating chemical reactions or enzymatic modifi-
cations. Moreover, ultrasonic treatment accelerates reaction rates through the creation of
local turbulence and high-pressure zones. This technique plays a crucial role in improving
gelation properties, allowing for precise control over gel structure and properties in soy
protein. Hence, ultrasonic technology emerges as a prime option for modifying soy protein,
opening up novel possibilities for its application in the food industry, pharmaceuticals and
various other domains.

Nowadays, SPI modification still faces several challenges, including ensuring consis-
tency of modification results, reducing cost and equipment complexity, and controllability
in large-scale production. In order to overcome these difficulties, it requires a combination
of process optimization, technological innovation and sustainability [9]. However, most
conventional sonication modifications have been performed on commercially or laboratory-
extracted SPI [10]. For example, Hu’s [11] study found that high-intensity sonication
of SPI increased its surface hydrophobicity and free sulfhydryl content, and promoted
the formation of gel networks. This is consistent with the findings of Zhang et al. [12]
who showed that the gel strength and water-holding properties of SPI were significantly
improved by 40 min of ultrasound pretreatment, and that the microstructure was more
uniform and dense. The effects on functional properties, such as protein gelation, have
not been further observed when sonication is performed during the extraction process.
Karki et al. [13] first subjected defatted soy flakes to ultrasonic treatment during soy protein
extraction, which resulted in enhanced release of proteins and sugars in the extract, leading
to increased yields of both components. However, they did not further investigate the
impact on protein gel properties. Moreover, ultrasonic modification of SPI after extraction
may lead to increased costs. Thus, the hypothesis is proposed that it would be possible to
modify SPI by combining ultrasound with the extraction process. To address these issues,
a series of experiments was conducted exploring the impact of introducing ultrasound
treatment at the alkali solubilization stage of SPI.

This work aimed to study the microstructural and physicochemical impact of ultra-
sound therapy at varying intensities and durations on the of SPI properties by combining
the alkaline solubilization stage of SPI extraction with ultrasonic treatment. Subsequently,
the effects of ultrasonication on its TGase-induced gel properties, including structure,
strength, water-holding capacity and rheological properties, were evaluated. Finally, the
mechanism of the difference between the traditional and current modification methods
of SPI by ultrasound was studied. This investigation not only illuminated the refined

extraction process but also underscored the benefits of incorporating ultrasound treatment
in the alkaline solubilization phase to augment the overall functional properties of SPI.

PROTEIN DENATURATION AND SOLUBILITY:
The FPI suspension (2% protein w/w) had a native pH of 7.3. The amount of soluble protein (colloidal protein fraction, derived after dispersing for 2 h at 40 °C with subsequent centrifugation) was analyzed to be 95% (18 mg/mL). Therefore, majority of the proteins of FPI were soluble in the studied conditions. Our previous results had indicated around 80% solubility for FPI ( Nivala et al., 2017 ), however, the samples were dispersed at room temperature, while in the current study 40 °C was used which may have led to increased solubility.
The secondary structural features of the native (non-heated) and heat-treated colloidal faba bean proteins were analyzed by CD. The far-UV CD spectra of the native FPI showed a broad shoulder at 210–220 nm and a positive peak around 195 nm ( Fig. 1 ). The broad negative shoulder at 210–220 nm indicates that the structure consists predominantly of parallel and anti-parallel β-sheet structures however the typical distinct negative peak at 216–218 nm associated with well-defined β-sheets was missing. The dominant β-sheet conformation is generally expected for legumins ( Choi & Ma, 2007 ; Clara Sze, Kshirsagar, Venkatachalam, & Sathe, 2007 ; Martínez-Velasco et al., 2018 ; Schwenke et al., 2000 ; Yin et al., 2010 ), though there are not many published studies on far-UV spectra of FPI. The protein composition of the FPI used in the current study comprised of legumin and vicilin polypeptides as well as higher MW proteins ( Nivala et al., 2017 ). The multi-protein nature of the plant material may inhibit collection of proper dichroic data. Liu et al. (2019b) recently reported the effect of TG-induced crosslinking on the far-UV spectra of a similar FPI preparation. A wide negative peak at 210–225 nm was evident which showed minor shifts after TG crosslinking at lower dosages than in the current study ( Liu et al., 2019b ). The far-UV CD spectra of the heat-treated (90 °C, 30 min) FPI sample showed a clear shift towards 200 nm and loss of positive peak around 195 nm ( Fig. 1 ). The shift clearly indicates the loss of ordered structures and the increase of random coil conformation and molecular flexibility. The spectrum for the heat-denatured FPI shows similarity with e.g. molten globule state of bovine β-lactoglobulin ( Ercili-Cura et al., 2012 ). The denaturation temperature of FPI was measured to be 94 °C by differential scanning calorimetry in our previous study ( Nivala et al., 2017 ). Thus, a partially unfolded structure is expected in the current heat treatment conditions.

ENZYMATIC CROSSLINKING OF THE HEAT-TREATED PROTEINS:
Enzyme treatment with 1000 nkat TG/g protein dosage caused efficient crosslinking of the faba bean proteins to large polymers (>250 kDa) identified by SDS-PAGE ( Fig. 2 ), which was also depicted in ( Nivala et al., 2017 ). FPI was composed mainly of legumin-like 11S proteins (α- and β-polypeptides). Faint bands of vicilin and convicilin were visible. The TG-induced crosslinking of the proteins was intensified after the heat treatment. When the heat-treated (90 °C, 30 min) FPI was incubated with TG, it was observed that both hydrophilic α- and hydrophobic β-polypeptides were crosslinked into large polymers ( Fig. 2 ). Whereas without the heat treatment, β-polypeptides of legumin-like 11S globulins, buried inside the core of the native proteins, stayed mainly intact after TG treatment. The change observed in the secondary structure of faba bean proteins i.e., partial denaturation and molten globule-like conformation formation may have facilitated efficient exposure of β-polypeptides to the enzyme and formation of inter-molecular γ-glutamyl-lysine isopeptide links. Neither heat treatment, nor TG-induced crosslinking caused a dramatic change in the amount of soluble proteins analyzed from the colloidal fraction (data not shown). The results indicate that the colloidal particles resisted extensive particle-particle interactions at the studied concentration of around 18 mg/mL in the colloidal fraction.

SURFACE HYDROPHOBICITY AND EMULSION PROPERTIES:
The surface hydrophobicity of colloidal FPI sample increased remarkably after the heat treatment (from 181 to 504 RFU) while the TG treatment caused a decrease in surface hydrophobicity of the heat-treated FPI from 504 to 435 RFU ( Table 1 ). Similarly, a decrease in surface hydrophobicity was observed for TG-treated native FPI. Increase in surface hydrophobicity after heat treatment is due to dissociation of subunits and partial unfolding of globulin structures exposing the buried hydrophobic sites. Similar increase in hydrophobicity was reported for e.g. soy protein isolate ( Wang, Li, Jiang, Qi, & Zhou, 2014 ). Decrease of surface hydrophobicity due to enzymatic crosslinking may be explained by decreased structural flexibility of colloidal proteins due to intra-molecular and intra-particle crosslinking ( Ercili-Cura et al., 2015 ; Nivala et al., 2017 ), meaning that crosslinking reduced availability of hydrophobic sites. ANS is a fluorescent probe, which binds to hydrophobic sites on the protein surface, while a second mechanism of binding involves electrostatic interaction between positively charged amino acid residues (involving lysine) and the negatively charged sulfonate group of ANS ( Johnston, Nickerson, & Low, 2015 ; Lee, 2010 ). Thus, possible change in spatial organization of the surface hydrophobic sites e.g. observed by loss of β-legumins into larger aggregates ( Fig. 2 ) and even loss of lysine residues into TG-induced formation of γ-glutamyl-lysine bonds may have caused reduction of surface hydrophobicity in crosslinked FPI samples.
The emulsion properties, EAI and ESI, were analyzed following the turbidity change in the bottom of the emulsion tubes ( Table 1 ). EAI values ranging between 25 and 30 m 2 /g were obtained for all the samples. A similar EAI range was reported for soy protein isolates at pH 6.5 by Pearce and Kinsella (1978) . For comparison, EAI values of 149 and 119 were reported for sodium caseinate and whey protein powder, respectively ( Pearce & Kinsella, 1978 ). Heat treatment caused a minor increase in EAI of FPI from 25.1 to 27.4 m 2 /g. TG treatment also caused increase of EAI in native faba bean proteins (up to 30.5 m 2 /g). EAI, is an index of the area stabilized per unit weight of protein, and it is a function of the oil volume fraction. Thus, EAI depends on the protein/oil ratio chosen for the study, and is also affected by the methodology and equipment used to prepare the emulsions ( Pearce & Kinsella, 1978 ). Therefore, making comparisons of EAI values between other reported values in literature is challenging. Based on the observed ESI values, no conclusions can be made on stability of the emulsions due to high standard deviations (>10%) observed for each case. ESI is reliable parameter only when ‘good enough’ emulsion is achieved. The emulsions generated in the current study were not stable in that respect. Similar value range, however, was reported for salt extracted faba bean, lupin, pea, chick pea and soybean protein stabilized emulsions by Can Karaca et al. (2011) and for faba bean proteins for emulsions generated with much lower protein/oil ratio. Johnston et al. (2015) reported improved creaming stability after crosslinking of faba bean proteins with genipin and hypothesized that the interface formed of crosslinked proteins would show higher resistance to destabilization. In addition, optimal (slight) reduction in solubility may provide a thicker interface with improved steric stability. We have previously reported around 70% reduction of protein solubility for native faba bean proteins when crosslinked with TG (1000 nkat/g protein) ( Nivala et al., 2017 ). In the current study, only colloidal protein fraction was used for heat and TG treatments and subsequent emulsification. The differences between EAI values have been minor indicating emulsions were stabilized by similar colloidal particles despite the heat and TG treatments in the studied conditions. No correlation between emulsion properties and surface hydrophobicity was possible either. It would be expected that increased surface hydrophobicity would improve emulsifying activity of proteins as hydrophobicity is one of the driving forces for adsorption of proteins to oil/water interface, however increased protein-protein interactions would be the limiting factor. Molina, Papadopoulou, and Ledward (2001) reported similar phenomena for high pressure treated soy protein 11S globulins at pH 6.5. It was indicated that surface hydrophobicity is more indicative for emulsifying properties in the case of highly soluble proteins, whereas for proteins with lower solubility, solubility is more important parameter ( Molina et al., 2001 ). Overall, emulsifying properties of FPI were not affected dramatically by the heat and TG treatments in the current conditions. It should be investigated further using other protein/oil ratios.

GEL FORMATION:

HEAT-INDUCED GELATION:
Rheological changes during heat treatment (90 °C, 5 min) of FPI dispersions at concentrations of 10 and 15% (w/w) were followed by small deformation oscillatory measurements performed during heating and cooling cycles ( Fig. 3 ). The whole FPI suspension without separation of the colloidal fraction was used for the gelation experiments. Despite a heat treatment duration of 30 min was used in the rest of the study, in-situ heating experiment was performed for an incubation period of 5 min (at 90 °C) using the plate-plate geometry to minimize the possible evaporation impact. It was observed that at both concentrations, the dispersions started to show gel-like characteristics (tanδ >1) at around 83 °C (30 min after the start of heating cycle). The denaturation temperature for FPI was shown to be 94 °C in our previous publication with onset of denaturation temperature being around 83 °C ( Nivala et al., 2017 ). Similar gelation temperature was reported for soy protein isolate ( Renkema & van Vliet, 2002 ). The modulus continued to increase during the cooling cycle and plateaued at around 25 °C (70 min after the start of heating-cooling cycle). At 10% concentration, FPI dispersion showed gel-like characteristics with a final storage modulus ( G′ ) value of 180 Pa. However, the sample was still easily flowing, thus it was possible to use that condition for acidification and TG-induced gelation subsequently. Increasing the protein concentration to 15% resulted in slight increase of final G′ to 230 Pa at the studied heating conditions ( Fig. 3 ). Higher G′ values were reported for 15% FPI gels at neutral pH when heat-treated at 95 °C, for 30 min and cooled back to room temperature ( Langton et al., 2020 ). It is known that gel stiffness correlates well with the degree of protein denaturation, i.e. the higher the degree of denaturation the higher the G′ of heat-induced gel for e.g. soy 11S globulins ( Renkema, Gruppen, & van Vliet, 2002 ; Renkema & van Vliet, 2002 ). With the heat treatment conditions used in the current study, stiff gels were not achieved at either protein concentration, as the degree of protein denaturation was not extensive. The main target for studying heat-induced changes in rheological properties of the 10 and 15% dispersions in the current study was to show the effects of pre-heat treatment at 90 °C on dispersion state before using such for the subsequent acid- and TG-induced gelation studies.

EMULSIFYING PROPERTIES:
Protein emulsifying agents should readily form oil-in-water emulsions with small droplet sizes and keep them stable over time. The emulsifying properties of HSPIs at pH 7.0 were evaluated by emulsifying activity index (EAI), emulsifying stability index (ESI), and average emulsion droplet size (Z-Ave) ( Fig. 4 ). Regardless of the isolation method, non-germinated HSPIs did not perform well as emulsifiers, exhibiting very low EAI values. Only hemp seed samples that underwent 5-days of germination were good emulsifiers. Long-term germination increased the EAI to 33.05 m 2 g −1 for G5-IP while UF further increased EAI to 36.48 m 2 g −1 for G5-UF, but both values were statistically similar. ESI was measured for each emulsion 48 h after formation, but when emulsions have a low EAI to start, such as for non-germinated and short-term germinated samples, the resulting ESI values are not meaningful. Again, G5-IP and G5-UF demonstrated very similar stability values of approximately 10%.
Z-Ave is another metric to evaluate an emulsion, since smaller droplets tend to remain stable over longer periods of time compared to larger droplets ( Damodaran, 2005 ). G5-IP and G5-UF formed emulsions with similar Z-Ave, showing their similarities in emulsion stability. This finding is in agreement with prior literature, which did not experience any significant change in emulsifying properties between IP and UF for pulse protein concentrates ( Boye et al., 2010 ). However, when UF was paired with hemp seed germination, Z-Ave decreases from 4.7 μm for G0-IP to 2.2 μm for G5-UF, a significant reduction in droplet size that reflects an improvement in emulsifying ability.
Protein composition and solubility, surface hydrophobicity, and aggregation state can all play a role in the emulsifying ability of a protein isolate ( Tang et al., 2006 ). Despite the lower solubility of G5-UF (6.74%) compared to G5-IP (18.45%) at pH 7.0, the two protein isolates exhibited similar EAI, ESI, and Z-Ave values. Their comparable emulsifying abilities are not well explained by surface hydrophobicity or aggregation behavior either. G5-IP has a surface hydrophobicity of 74.5 arbitrary units, while G5-UF has a value of 120.2 ( Table S2 ). The two protein isolates also form soluble aggregates of similar size at pH 7.0 ( Fig. S2 ). Different composition and physicochemical properties between G5-IP and G5-UF, and their similarities in emulsifying properties, suggest that small peptide fragments that are removed during UF are inconsequential for forming and stabilizing emulsions. Alternatively, non-protein components in a protein isolate can sometimes aid in stabilizing emulsion droplets ( Malomo et al., 2014 ). We did observe a correlation between the low protein purity of G5-IP and G5-UF (87.61 and 87.86%) and high EAI, and further studies regarding the nature of the non-proteinaceous components in the protein isolate its impact on EAI should be explored.

GELLING PROPERTIES:
In order to replace gelled animal-protein foods, such as yogurt and cooked eggs, plant protein ingredients should form gels at various concentrations. The gelling properties of HSPI depended on the extent of germination and protein isolation method ( Table 3 ). Least gelation concentration (LGC) was similar among G0-IP, G3-IP, and G5-IP samples at 2 w/v%, with G1-IP exhibiting a slightly higher LGC at 2.5 w/v%. Previous findings reported that 1-day germinated HSPIs experienced an increased LGC due to the lower concentration of protein in the isolate ( Liu et al., 2023a ). Yet, in this study, the concentration of protein in G1-IP is equivalent to G3-IP, which did not experience any change in LGC. Instead, the protein modifications that occurred in early-stage germination may have affected the hemp seed protein structure in a way that weakens its ability to crosslink and form gel networks.
UF diminished the ability of germinated HSPI to form gels at low concentrations. G0-UF and G1-UF did not experience a change in LGC, but LGC values increased for G3-UF (4 w/v%) and G5-UF (6 w/v%) from their IP counterparts (2 w/v%). Since UF removed the smallest peptides from G3 and G5 protein isolates and dramatically increased their LGC, it may be inferred that these small proteins were integral to gel formation at low concentrations, a finding which is supported by a previous study ( Bi et al., 2014 ). At the same time, large storage proteins that compose most of G0-UF and G1-UF are no longer present in high concentrations in G3-UF and G5-UF due to protein mobilization and degradation. With the smallest peptides lost to UF and the largest proteins degraded from long-term germination, G3-UF and G5-UF contained only mid-sized protein components that were less capable of forming gel networks, thus their increases in LGC.

Modifying proteins with new methods to improve their functional properties is essential to extend their application in food related field. In this study, the effect of pH-shifting treatment on structural and heat induced gel properties of peanut protein isolate (PPI) were investigated. PPI was subject to different pH conditions (pH 2, pH 4, pH 10, and pH 12) for 1 h, then adjusted back to pH 7 and they were marked as PPI2, PPI4, PPI10, and PPI12, respectively. It was found that the breaking force (BF) and water holding capacity (WHC) of PPI10 gel were significantly improved due to the decreased particle size, increased solubility, free sulfhydryl group content and surface hydrophobicity of PPI10. While PPI2 or PPI12 lost their gel ability due to the formation of large protein aggregates. These results indicated that pH-shifting treatment might be a convenient and economical method to prepare PPI with different gel and structural properties.

KEYWORDS: Peanut protein isolate; pH-shifting; Gel properties; Structure

EMULSIFYING ACTI V ITY INDEX (EAI) AND EMULSIFYING STABILITY INDEX (ESI):
The emulsifying activity index and emulsifying stability index were determined following the method of Wang et al. (2021) , with slight modifications. 3 mL of 0.1 % ( w / v ) pepper seed protein isolate solution was mixed with 3 mL of pepper seed oil. The solution was homogenized with a homogenizer for 2 min at a speed of 12,000 rpm. 50 μL of the emulsion was quickly taken from the bottom of the obtained emulsion and added to 5 mL of a 0.1 % SDS solution, mixed well. The absorbance value (A 0 ) at 500 nm was then measured using the 0.1 % SDS solution as a blank to calculate the emulsifying activity. After standing for 10 min, the above procedure was repeated to determine the absorbance value (A 10 ) to calculate the emulsion stability. The EAI and ESI of PSPI under different treatment conditions were calculated using the following formulas: (4) EAI m 2 / g = 2 T × D × A 0 / C × ϕ × 100000 (5) ESI % = A 10 / A 0 × 100 % where T is a constant (2.303); D is the dilution ratio; C is the protein concentration, g/mL; ϕ is the volume fraction of the oil, %.

FOAMING CHARACTERISTICS (FC) AND FOAMING STABILITY (FS):
The foaming characteristics and foaming stability were determined following the method of Zhang et al. (2012) , with slight modifications. The pepper seed protein isolate solution with a concentration of 10 mg/mL was prepared, and 4 mL of the solution was homogenized for 2 min at a speed of 10,000 rpm. The resulting foam was quickly transferred to a 10 mL cylinder. The initial foam volume ( V 0 ) at 0 min was recorded to calculate the foaming property. After standing for 30 min, the residual foam volume (V 1 ) was recorded to calculate the foaming stability. The FC and FS of PSPI under different treatment conditions were calculated using the following formulas: (6) FC % = V 0 / 4 × 100 % (7) FS % = V 0 / V 1 × 100 %

RHEOLOGICAL PROPERTIES:
The rheological properties were determined using a TA DHR-2 Rheometer (TA Instruments, USA) following the method of Xu et al. (2020) , with slight modification. The PSPI solutions were prepared with distilled water, and measurements were conducted at ambient temperature. A plate fixture, measuring 40 mm in diameter with a 1 mm clearance, was utilized to achieve a gap of 400 μm between the plate and platform. The shear rate ranged from 0.1 s −1 and 1000 s −1 . The rheological properties of the pepper seed protein isolate solution were evaluated through flow slope analysis. The study aimed to establish the relationship between shear stress and shear rate, as well as the impact of shear rate on viscosity. The results were then analyzed using rheometer software.

STATISTICAL ANALYSIS:
All experiments were conducted in triplicate. Statistical analysis was conducted following the method of El-Hadary et al. (2023) . Results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). A P value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS 19.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA).

Imbalances between global supply and demand for protein sources are becoming apparent as the global population grows rapidly. Accordingly, the demand for plant-based meat has increased significantly to address concerns related to global public health, animal welfare, and environmental sustainability ( Greis et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022a ). Soybean and pea proteins are widely used as raw materials in plant-based meats because of their superior nutritional and functional properties, including their emulsification and gelation capacities ( Boye, Zare, & Pletch, 2010; Zhao, Shen, Wu, Zhang & Xu, 2020 ). Nevertherless, these proteins have several drawbacks. These legume proteins contain food allergens and antinutrients (isoflavones and trypsin inhibitors) that can cause digestive disorders, such as nausea, diarrhea, and indigestion ( Savage, Kaeding, Matsui, & Wood, 2010; Taylor et al., 2021 ). In addition, the flavor of the raw ingredients can affect the final flavor of plant-based meats, thereby decreasing their consumer appeal ( Wang et al., 2021; Youssef et al., 2020 ). Thus, many attempts have been made to replace soybean protein with other plant proteins ( Malomo, He, & Aluko, 2014; Nie, Liu, Jiang, Xiong, & Zhao, 2022 ).
Mung beans ( Vigna radiata L. ) are an important edible legume crop widely cultivated in Southeast Asia, South America, Australia, and Africa. They can be economically cultivated in dry climates and are rich in proteins (21.0 % to 31.3 %), essential amino acids, minerals, and vitamins B and C ( Anwar, Latif, Przybylski, Sultana, & Ashraf, 2007 ). Furthermore, mung bean protein isolate (MBPI) is easily digested compared to other legumes and is relatively low-cost ( Hou et al., 2019 ). Based on these benefits, MBPIs are currently attracting attention as raw materials for plant-based meats ( Liu et al., 2021; Yi-Shen, Shuai, & Fitzgerald, 2018 ). However, the applications of MBPI to foods are limited due to its poorer functional properties compared to soybean protein isolate ( Ratnawati, Desnilasari, Surahman, & Kumalasari, 2019 ). In particular, the gelation properties and fibrous structure of proteins can affect the texture of the final product, which depends on melting and cooling processes within the extruder ( Lin et al., 2022 ).
Various structural modification methods, including chemical, enzymatic, and physical methods, have been used to attempt to improve the techno-functional properties of MBPIs. Each method has its advantages and limitations ( Chen & Campanella, 2022; Luo, Yang, Wang, Ashokkumar, & Hemar, 2022; Wang et al., 2023a ). pH-shifting is an eco-friendly and simple method for modifying protein structures without the need for chemical reagents or expensive equipment. Under extreme pH conditions (alkaline or acidic), protein interactions (including van der Waals forces and hydrophobic interactions between protein molecules) are destroyed by strong electrostatic repulsions. Subsequently, globular proteins become flexible, adopting “molten globule” structures due to the cleavage of chemical bonds. These structures can be partially refolded, and new protein structures can be maintained at neutral pH. The neutralized proteins from the molten globule state possess increased solubility, surface hydrophobicity, and flexible secondary structures (random coils), thereby improving the flexibility of the overall protein structure ( Jiang et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2021 ). The exposure of buried amino acid residues and increased protein solubility may improve the techno-functional properties of modified proteins. Many researchers have reported that pH-shifting improves the gelation properties of legume protein-derived gels, including pea, peanut, and soybean proteins, by changing their structure ( Jiang, Xiong, & Chen, 2010; Li et al., 2020; Zhu, Huang, Guo, & Chen, 2021 ). Additionally, some studies have assessed emulsion gels derived from MBPI treated with pH-shifting at pH 12 ( Nie et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022a ). However, these studies only focused on the phenomenological enhancement of gel properties without structural analyses and were limited to MBPI treated with pH-shifting at pH 12, without considering other pHs. With a comparison of acidic and alkaline pH-shifting, the main structural differences that impact the techno-functional properties of MBPI treated by pH-shifting should be identified to understand the principle of their improvement. Furthermore, different degrees of electrostatic repulsion can lead to noticeable structural changes, such as the disruption of protein units ( Li et al., 2020 ).
The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of pH-shifting on the structural properties, water holding capacity, and gelation propertiesof MBPI. Considering that excessively high or low pH-shifting could decrease protein purity, we assessed the effects of pH-shifting (from pH 2 to pH 12) on MBPI. To study pH-shifting-induced structural changes in the modified MBPIs, they were subjected to structural and physicochemical analyses, including surface hydrophobicity, free sulfhydryl and disulfide bond contents, FT-IR, secondary structure contents, and SDS-PAGE analyses. Also, we evaluated the water holding capacity and gel formation ability (least gelation concentration) of modified MBPI treated by pH-shifting. Finally, through rheological and morphological analyses, the gel properties of heat-induced gels derived from pH-shifting-modified MBPI were measured to survey the impact of increased water holding capacity on their gelation properties.

molecular weight distribution of the proteins recovered in
SCKPC and the electrophoretogram generated is presented

Production and composition of SCKPC

The water holding capacity is regarded as an indicator of
the ability of a protein to physically hold water against
gravity (Kinsella 1981). WHC is a crucial functional
property for highly viscous foodstuffs such as soups,
doughs, gravies, sauces, and bakery products. The water-
holding ability of the protein molecule is a function of size,
shape, hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions. Further-
more, water holding capacity is affected by lipid and car-
bohydrate content, and the properties of amino acid
residues on the surface (Damodaran 1997).

The WHC of SCKPC was 2.42 ± 0.09 g water/g
(242%), being higher than those of pea protein isolate
(1.7 g/g), broad bean protein isolate (1.8 g/g), soy protein

protein concentrate (1.74 g/g) (Ogunwolu et al. 2009), and
apricot kernel protein concentrate (1.40 g/g) (Sharma et al.

concentrate (2.70 g/g) (Martinez-Flores et al. 2006), and
various rice bran protein concentrates (3.87–5.60 g/g)
(Chandi and Sogi 2007). Water holding capacity is a useful

Oil holding capacity

Foam formation and properties are inﬂuenced by the type
of protein, preparation method, composition, solubility,
concentration, pH, the presence of salts and hydrophobic
interactions.
Moreover,
molecular
elasticity,
surface
hydrophobicity, charge distribution and hydrodynamic
properties affect foam formation and stability (Kinsella
1981). Foaming capacity depends on the diffusion of sol-
uble proteins toward the air–water interface, rapid con-
formational change and rearrangement at the interface
(Damodaran 1997). Therefore, ﬂexible protein molecules
have a good foaming capacity. On the other hand, globular
proteins, whose surface denaturation is very difﬁcult, have
low foaming capacity.

The interaction between protein and lipids determines the
sensory qualities of many foods. These interactions are
inﬂuenced by pH, ionic strength, temperature and the other
variables in the system. Proteins with low solubility and
high hydrophobicity can hold oil in large quantities
(Damodaran 1997). High oil holding is essential for some
food systems such as sausages, cake batters, mayonnaise
and salad dressings (Chandi and Sogi 2007).

protein molecule (Subagio 2006; Kaur and Singh 2007).
According to these results, there may be similar amount of
hydrophobic groups on the surface of sour cherry proteins
and casein molecules.

Soy is a source of the predominant vegetable proteins. Soy protein isolates (SPI) are
generally produced from soybean by being collected as precipitated curd in the acidic
condition [1], and SPI are essential for a wide range of protein-based food formulations [2,3],
owing to their outstanding processing ability, high nutritional value, and low cost. The
functional properties of SPI, such as solubility and emulsifying properties, are determined
by the protein composition, structure, degree of denaturation, and aggregation. According
to the needs in the speciﬁc food system, those properties can be modiﬁed by chemical,
physical, or enzymatic methods [4].

High hydrostatic pressure (HHP) technology is a non-thermal food-processing method
showing potential for the development of new food products with additional functional
and health beneﬁt [5]. Under HHP, proteins are regulated by the Le Chatelier’s principle
and shifted to a lower volume conformer, which in turn changes their structure and
conformation and inﬂuences their functional properties [6,7]. A number of researchers
have studied the impact of HHP treatment on SPI in recent years and found that solubility,
water holding capacity, and foaming property could be improved under medium-high
pressure (up to 400 MPa) for short processing time (5–20 min), while these properties
tend to decline under ultra-high pressure (above 400 MPa) [8–10]. Li et al. conﬁrmed

Plant protein replaced food products have received great attention lately due to the
increasing consumer awareness about the impacts of animal-based food production on the
environment and health beneﬁts of plant protein over animal protein, e.g., lowering blood
cholesterol level [12,13]. Soybean has been especially a popular source for plant-based
yogurt recently, because of its accessibility and quality. Previous studies suggested that
soy-based media might possess sufﬁcient substrates to promote the growth of probiotic
microorganisms [14,15]. However, the main problems with this type of product are appear-
ance and texture caused by phase separation and the off-ﬂavor of the plant material [16].
Besides combinations of gelling agents, improving the functional properties of proteins,
especially increasing the stabilization of soy proteins on acidiﬁed food systems, may be
a solution [17]. For the ﬂavor of soybean products, controlling its Lipoxygenase (LOX)
activity is very important, since it is responsible for the generation of a series of off-ﬂavor
components in soybean and soy-derived products. As mentioned earlier, modiﬁed by
HHP can improve the functional properties of SPI, thus improving the quality of soybean
products. To the best of our knowledge, this research revealed an application of modiﬁed
soy proteins in yogurt for the ﬁrst time.

The main purpose of this work is to use HHP treatment to improve the functional
properties of SPI and apply it in producing soy-based yogurt. Response surface method-
ology was used to optimize the HHP process to modify the functional properties of SPI,
including solubility, water holding capacity (WHC), and emulsifying activity index (EAI).
A SPI-milk mixed yogurt was then produced, and its physicochemical and rheological
properties, as well as the volatile ﬂavor compounds characteristics, were evaluated.

MATERIALS AND REAGENTS:
Raw sunflower seeds with shells removed were procured from a market in Bayannur City, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, China. The sunflower seeds were subjected to cold pressing and defatting using a small-screw oil press (LTP218 Lagrange kitchenware, Shenzhen, China). The process was performed twice at 70 °C, resulting in a residual oil content of 8.76 % in the sunflower seed cake, which was subsequently crushed for use. Analytical grade reagents including n-hexane, isopropyl alcohol, butane, sodium hydroxide, and hydrochloric acid were used in this study and were purchased from Thermo Fisher Biochemical Products (Beijing) Co.

DEFATTING AND PROTEIN PREPARATION:
Sunflower seed cake was subjected to various protein extraction methods to produce sunflower seed meal protein (SPM), sunflower seed protein concentrate (SPC), and sunflower seed protein isolate (SPI). The sunflower seed cake obtained was first defatted using different solvents (n-hexane, isopropyl alcohol, and subcritical butane) at a ratio of 1:7 ( w / v ) and a temperature of 60 °C for 50 min per cycle. The subcritical butane extraction process involved placing the sunflower seed cake in a sealed subcritical extraction tank (CBE-20 L, Henan Subcritical Extraction Technology Research Institute Co., Ltd.), injecting butane, and extracting under reduced pressure. The resulting defatted sunflower seed meal protein (SPM) was then dried under a ventilator for 24 h and crushed through an 80-mesh sieve to obtain n-hexane extracted sunflower seed meal protein (SPM-h), isopropyl alcohol extracted sunflower seed meal protein (SPM-i) and subcritical butane extracted sunflower seed meal protein (SPM-b), respectively. The SPM was then stirred with 70 % ethanol at a ratio of 1:10 for 1.5 h at 50 °C and centrifuged (6000 rpm, 10 min). The precipitate was stirred with 95 % ethanol (1:10, w /w) for 1.5 h at 50 °C, centrifuged (6000 rpm, 10 min), and separated. The precipitate was then dried naturally to obtain sunflower seed protein concentrate (SPC), which was designated as SPC-h, SPC-i, and SPC-b, respectively. The SPC was then adjusted to a pH of 9.5 with 1 M NaOH (1:10, w /w), stirred for 2 h (300 rpm), centrifuged (4500 rpm, 15 min), adjusted to a pH of 4.3–4.5 with 1 M HCl, stirred for 30 min, centrifuged(4500 rpm, 15 min), precipitated to adjust the pH to 7, freeze-dried to obtain sunflower seed protein isolate (SPI), and designated as SPI-h, SPI-i and SPI-b respectively. The purity of each protein was: SPM-h 50.72 ± 0.48, SPM-i 52.55 ± 0.05, SPM-b 51.11 ± 0.08, SPC-h 61.82 ± 0.04, SPC-i 61.51 ± 0.03, SPC-b 61.63 ± 0.08, SPI-h 89.34 ± 0.02, SPI-i 89.69 ± 0.10, SPI-b 89.33 ± 0.06.

STRUCTURAL CHARACTERIZATION OF SUNFLOWER SEED PROTEIN:

SDS-PAGE:
The method described by Li et al. [ 21 ] was followed. Protein sample (4 mg/mL) was prepared by adding sample buffer, and the gels used for SDS-PAGE analysis were 5 % concentrated gel and 12 % separator gel. The operating conditions were electrophoresis at 30 V for 1.5 h and then transferred to 60 V for 2 h. Staining was performed using Thomas Brilliant Blue R250. The decolorizing solution was used with methanol-ice acetic acid solution and Mini-PROTEAN® system (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) was used to scan the electrophoresis membranes and perform photographic analysis.

FTIR:
The KBr tablet method was employed for determination, with 64 scans performed (400–4000 cm −1 wave number, 2 cm −1 resolution) (TENSOR 27, Germany). Relative proportions of protein secondary structure in the amide I band (1700–1600 cm −1 ) were calculated using Fourier self-inverse convolution, second-order derivative analysis, and curve fitting [ 22 ].

ENDOGENOUS FLUORESCENCE SPECTRUM:
The endogenous fluorescence of the samples was measured using an F-2500 fluorescence spectrophotometer (Hitachi, Japan) by the method proposed by Liu [ 23 ]. After thorough mixing of a 10 mg/mL protein aqueous solution (pH 7.0), the supernatant (6000 ×g, 15 min) was obtained by centrifugation and diluted to 0.25 mg/mL. Protein content was measured with an excitation wavelength of 290 nm, a scanning speed of 300 nm/s, a range of 300–450 nm, and a slit width of 2.5 nm.

SURFACE HYDROPHOBICITY ANALYSIS (H 0 ) AND PROTEIN WETTABILITY:
Sunflower seed protein solution (1 %, w / v ) was configured using phosphate buffers, mixed thoroughly and centrifuged for supernatants (6000 × g , 25 °C, 20 min), and measured the protein content. The supernatant was diluted with phosphate buffer to 0.04–0.5 mg/mL. Then, 20 μL of 8 mmol ANS solution was added to 4 mL of sample solution and mixed well, protected from light for 10 min. The hydrophobicity of the samples was determined using a fluorescence spectrophotometer (Hitachi F-2500) with an excitation wavelength of 390 nm and an emission wavelength of 470 nm. Surface hydrophobicity (H 0 ) was determined as the initial slope of the fluorescence intensity (vertical axis) versus the protein concentration (horizontal axis) curve [ 24 ].

SEM:
The microstructure of the sunflower seed protein was determined by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (SU8010, Hitachi, Japan). Sunflower seed proteins were evenly distributed on the conductive tape, and gold was sprayed for detection at an accelerated voltage of 10 kV [ 25 ].

COARSE EMULSION MICROSTRUCTURE:
We followed Hei et al.'s method [ 26 ] to determine the emulsification as per the method described in 2.5.3. A fresh emulsion was prepared and 20 μL of Nile red and Nile blue were added. The emulsion was then stained for 10 min in the dark. The dyed emulsion was placed on the carrier platform, and the microstructure of the emulsion was observed by laser confocal microscopy at excitation wavelengths of 488 nm and 633 nm.

PROPERTY ANALYSIS OF SUNFLOWER SEED PROTEIN:

THERMAL CHARACTERISTIC ANALYSIS:
According to a study conducted by Liu et al. [ 23 ], 3 mg of protein was weighed and placed in an aluminum container along with 10 μL of ultra-pure water. The container was then sealed and maintained overnight at 4 °C. The determination was performed using a differential scanning calorimeter (DSC) (TA Q20, New Castle, USA) with a scanning temperature ranging from 30 °C to 120 °C and a scanning rate of 10 °C/min. An empty aluminum container was used as a blank control.

RHEOLOGICAL PROPERTIES:
The linear viscoelastic region of the protein was measured at 1 Hz. The test was performed in the linear viscoelastic range, with an angular frequency range of 0.1–100 rad/s, and a plate diameter of 40 mm (HR-2, TA, New Castle, USA). The strain amplitude in the test was set as 1 %. The apparent viscosity of the protein samples was measured at 25 °C and 1.0–100 s −1 shear rate [ 27 ].

In this paper, a JRBP-CC complex was prepared after ultrasound treatment of JRBP. The results showed that, compared with IRBP, the secondary structure of JRBP was very different, and it had a higher WHC content and better emulsification performance. After ultrasound processing, the secondary structure of the protein was gradually unfolded, and the particle size of JRBP-CC was small and well dispersed in the CLSM image. When the ultrasound power was 200 W, the λ max of the JRBP-CC showed a redshift, the particle size was the smallest, the absolute value of the zeta potential was the largest, the hydrophobicity was the strongest, and the emulsification and oxidation resistance were the best. This discovery seeks to promote the application of JRBP-CC in the food industry to provide economic and social benefits.

PROXIMATE COMPOSITION:
The proximate composition of the seed flours (dwb) is summarized in Table 1 . Tree nut and oilseeds contained low moisture (range – 1.53 ± 0.20 g/100 g for macadamia to 8.39 ± 0.07 g/100 g for soybeans) and high lipid (range – 21.88 ± 0.10 g/100 g for soybean to 67.63 ± 0.40 g/100 g for macadamia). Ash content of the tested seeds was in a narrow range (1.08 ± 0.21 g/100 g for pistachio to 3.48 ± 0.23 g/100 g for sesame). Dry beans and cereals were rich in carbohydrates (>70 g/100 g). Rice contained the highest (89.78 ± 0.71 g/100 g) and walnut the lowest (12.89 ± 0.00 g/100 g) amount of carbohydrates in the tested seeds. Among the tested seeds, peanuts (25.41 ± 0.18 g/100 g) and soybeans (31.48 ± 0.76 g/100 g) had the highest protein content. These data are consistent with the reported chemical composition of the selected seeds ( Davis, Cain, Peters, Le Tourneau, & McGinnis, 1981; Deshpande et al., 1984; Doughty & Walker, 1982; Hayat, Ahmad, Masud, Ahmed, & Bashir, 2014; Namiki, 1995; Ravindran, 1991; USDA, 2014; Venkatachalam & Sathe, 2006 ).

COLOR:
Rice flour had the lightest color followed by chickpea, sesame, pearl millet, and wheat as indicated by their respective ( L *) value ( Table 2 ). Defatting typically improved the L * value as lipid soluble pigments (e.g. carotenoids, xanthophylls, and chlorophylls) could be removed with the seed flour lipid removal. Among tree nuts, almond, Brazil nut, hazel nut, pecan and walnut exhibited redness (positive a * values). Similarly peanut, chickpeas, wheat, pearl millet and soybeans registered measurable redness. The yellowness of pistachio flour was the highest ( b * = 41.96 ± 0.26) and that of the black gram flour was the lowest ( b * = 10.00 ± 0.15). In all tested flours redness was lower than yellowness. Defatting helped reduce the redness and yellowness in all flours. Bookwalter, Kwolek, Black, and Griffin (1971) have reported similar effects of defatting on soybean flour color.

BULK DENSITY:
Bulk density ( Fig. 1 ) varied over a wide range (0.179 g/cm 3 for defatted pecan flour to 0.930 g/cm 3 for full fat black gram flour) and is in agreement with reported bulk density for a variety of seed flours that include: yellow (32 g/100 g lipid) and brown (35 g/100 g lipid) tigernut flours-respective bulk density of 0.62 g/cm 3 and 0.55 g/cm 3 ( Oladele & Aina, 2007 ); soybean flour (bulk density 0.5598 g/cm 3 ) ( Padilla, Alvarez, & Alfaro, 1996 ); adzuki bean (0.62 g/cm 3 ), rice bean (0.59 g/cm 3 ) and Indian bean (0.64 g/cm 3 ) flours ( Chau & Cheung, 1998 ); 0.536–0.562 g/cm 3 for Desi chickpeas and 0.571 g/cm 3 for Kabuli chickpea ( Kaur & Singh, 2005 ). The observed decreased bulk density in the current investigation upon defatting would be useful when light flours with more volume are desired. In case of flours with low lipid content (black gram, chickpea, rice, wheat, and pearl millets) decrease in bulk density as a result of defatting was minimal and therefore using the defatted form of these flours may not offer significant advantage in terms of product volume. Bulk density of several millet flours has been reported to be partly dependent on the grain moisture content ( Subramanian & Viswanathan, 2007 ). Egbekun and Ehieze (1997) suggested that using the defatted sesame flour, due to its low bulk density, would be an advantage in infant food formulations. In the current investigation, with the exception of Brazil nut, bulk density was higher for flours with higher moisture content. Upon defatting, we observed the bulk density of cashew nut flour to decrease from 0.536 g/cm 3 to 0.412 g/cm 3 . Our results for cashew nut flour bulk density are in agreement with a cashew nut flour bulk density decrease (from 0.34–0.47 g/cm 3 to 0.27–0.40 g/cm 3 ) reported by Fagbemi (2008) . A decrease in bulk density from 0.51 to 0.40 and 0.57 to 0.37 g/cm 3 , respectively for dehulled orange seed ( Akpata & Akubor, 1999 ) and pumpkin seed ( Rodríguez-Miranda et al., 2012 ) flours has also been reported.
Particle size and packing density are two major contributing factors in determining the bulk density of seed flours. In the presence of lipids, particles may pack closer as the triglycerides may act as adhesives in agglomeration of carbohydrate and protein molecules (either alone or together) permitting higher bulk density. During seed grinding, presence of lipids may interfere in particle size reduction as lipids can act as lubricants as well as help hold water molecules possibly by polar interactions between the ester bonds of triglycerides and polar water molecules. A combined effect of the two may partly explain why full fat flours tend to exhibit higher bulk density than their corresponding defatted counterparts. Particle adhesion during grinding oilseeds (e.g. peanut, soybean, sesame and tree nuts) poses difficulty in obtaining uniform particle sized full fat flours and warrants further investigations.

MATERIALS:
Chinese quince ( Chaenomeles speciose ; family Rosaceae) seeds were purchased from a local market, and the seeds were produced in Sichuan, China. The protein molecular weight standards were purchased from Thermo Fishier Scientific, USA; all other reagents and chemicals were of analytical grade.

PREPARATION OF CHINESE QUINCE SEED PROTEIN ISOLATE:
The method used to extract and purify Chinese quince seed protein isolate (CPI) referred to a previous report ( Timilsena, Adhikari, Barrow, & Adhikari, 2016 ) with some modifications. After husking, Chinese quince seeds were ground into flour. Next, the flour was defatted using a Soxhlet unit. The flour was mixed with petroleum ether in a 1:10 ratio (w/v) and was continuously extracted for 12 h at 45 °C. The defatted flour was air-dried until the solvent was totally evaporated.
The defatted Chinese quince seed flour was dispersed in water using a solid-liquid ratio of 1:10 (w/v), and the pH of this slurry was adjusted to 10 to extract the protein using 1 M NaOH. To facilitate solubilizing, the slurry was stirred using a mechanical stirrer at room temperature for 2 h. The slurry was centrifuged at 10,000 g for 20 min, and the supernatant containing protein was collected. To obtain a high yield, this procedure was repeated on the residue to obtain additional protein. The combined supernatant was acidified to a pH of 4.2 (isoelectric point) by adding 1 M HCl to precipitate the dissolved protein. The precipitated protein was recovered by high speed centrifugation and washed with distilled water three times (3 × 40 ml). The recovered protein was resuspended in distilled water and neutralized to a pH of 7 by adding 1 M NaOH. The protein suspension was dried by freeze-drying. Freeze-drying was performed in a laboratory freeze drier (Wizard 2.0, Virtis, USA). The protein suspension was first frozen at −30 °C for 6 h and dried at −10 °C for 72 h, and finally, the sample was dried at 25 °C for 4 h. The freeze-dried Chinese quince seed protein isolate was collected, pulverized to pass through a 180 μm sieve and stored at 4 °C.

PHYSICOCHEMICAL PROPERTIES:

DETERMINATION OF CHEMICAL COMPONENTS OF CHINESE QUINCE SEED AND CPI:
The protein content of Chinese quince seed before and after defatting was measured by Combustion Nitrogen Analysis (N × 6.25). The moisture, ash, and fat contents of CPI were determined using the Association of Official Analytical Chemists procedures 925.1, 923.03 and 920.85, respectively ( AOAC, 2000 ). The protein content was measured via Combustion Nitrogen Analysis (N × 6.25).

AMINO ACID COMPOSITION:
The amino acid composition of CPI was determined according to a previous report from Rezig et al. (2013) , with slight modifications. First, 20 mg CPI samples were accurately weighed and placed in dry tubes, and then, 4 ml of 6 M HCl was added to each tube. Next, the tested tubes were air-exhausted and the CPI samples were hydrolyzed at 110 °C for 24 h.
Direct hydrochloric acid hydrolysis would result in an underestimation of cystine content due to its instability ( Spindler, Stadler, & Tanner, 1984 ). For determination of cystine in CPI, cystine needs to be stabilized by oxidation before acid hydrolysis. Briefly, 20 mg CPI samples were mixed with 2 ml of performic acid (containing formic acid/30% hydrogen peroxide (19:1, v/v)), and the mixture was put in an ice bath to react for 16 h. After that, 0.3 ml of 48% HBr was added to terminate the reaction. The resulting oxidized CPI samples were vacuum-dried and then transferred to HCl hydrolysis.
After the acid hydrolysis, samples were cooled and transfer into a 50 ml volumetric flask using distilled water. 2 ml of solution was taken and vacuum-dried, and the residues were redissolved using 2 ml of distilled water and vacuum-dried, and this procedure was repeated 3 times. Finally, the dried samples were dissolved in 2 ml citrate buffer (pH 2.2, 0.55 M trisodium citrate). After centrifugation, the supernatant was analyzed by an automatic amino-acid analyzer L-8800 (Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan) for determination of amino acid composition. External standard method was used to quantify by using standard amino acid solutions.
Tryptophan can be destroyed by acid hydrolysis. Therefore, the determination of tryptophan for CPI was conducted separately using sodium hydroxide to hydrolyze the CPI samples. The hydrolysis procedure and analysis method were performed according to previous report from Spies (1967) . The amino acid contents were expressed as g amino acid/100 g protein.

MEASUREMENT OF ZETA POTENTIAL:
The zeta potential of CPI was measured based on the method of Kaushik et al. (2016) . The CPI aqueous solutions (0.5%, w/v) were prepared by dispersing the protein samples in 0.1 M tris buffer (pH = 8.6). The solutions were filtrated through Whatman No. 1 filter paper, and the filtrated solutions were diluted 100 times with distilled water. The pH of these diluted solutions was adjusted in the range of 2–10 with 0.1 M HCl or 0.1 M NaOH. The zeta potential was determined using a Zeta Size Nano ZS instrument (Malvern Instrument Ltd., UK).

SODIUM DODECYL SULFATE-POLYACRYLAMIDE GEL ELECTROPHORESIS (SDS-PAGE):
Non-reducing and reducing SDS-PAGE were performed in a discontinuous buffer system with a 12.5% separating gel and 5% stacking gel based on the report of Laemmli (1970) with a few modifications. The CPI samples for reducing were solubilized in 0.05 M Tris-HCl buffer containing 1% SDS, 0.01% bromophenol blue, 10% glycerol, and 1% 2-mercaptoethanol or without 2-mercaptoethanol for non-reducing condition. The samples were boiled at 100 °C for 5 min. After cooling to ambient temperature, 10 μl of samples were applied to each lane. The electrophoresis was performed using a constant current of 15 mA in the stacking gel and 25 mA in the separating gel in Mini Protean Tera (Bio-Rad, USA). The gel was stained in 0.1% Coomassie brilliant blue (R-250) in an acetic acid/ethanol/water solution and destained in decolorizing agent (acetic acid/methanol/water, 10:20:70). The image was subsequently captured by using Gel imaging system Doc XR+ (Bio-Rad, USA), and the white light tranilluminator was used to obtain clear image.

THERMAL PROPERTIES:
The thermal properties of CPI were analyzed according to the method of Shevkani et al. (2015) , with some modifications. Briefly, CPI samples were dispersed in distilled water at a concentration of 15% (w/w) and stored at 4 °C overnight until analysis. The dispersions were accurately weighed and hermetically sealed in an aluminum pan. The sealed pan was scanned by a differential scanning calorimeter (DSC 8500, PerkinElmer, USA) from 30 to 140 °C at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. An empty pan was used as a reference.

DETERMINATION OF SURFACE HYDROPHOBICITY (S 0 ):
The surface hydrophobicity was analyzed according to the method of Kato and Nakai (1980) using sodium 8-anilino-1-naphthalenesulfonate (ANS) as the hydrophobic fluorescent probe. First, the CPI sample was dispersed in 0.01 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) with stirring for 30 min and then centrifuged. The concentration of protein in the supernatant was measured using the Bradford method, and the protein solution was serially diluted with concentrations ranging from 50 to 250 μg/ml. Next, 4 ml protein solutions at each concentration were taken, and 50 μl of 8 mM ANS solution (prepared in 0.01 M phosphate buffer, pH 7.0) was added to the diluted solutions; The fluorescence intensity (FI) of the samples was determined at 385 nm (excitation) and 480 nm (emission) via an LS 55 fluorescence spectrophotometer (PerkinElmer, USA) with an emission slit of 5 nm. The FI of the ANS solution and each diluted sample solution without probe were also determined as controls, as was the initial slope of the FI value versus protein concentration plot, as a calculated linear regression.

FREE SULFHYDRYL GROUP (SH) AND DISULFIDE BOND (SS) CONTENTS MEASUREMENTS:
The sulfhydryl groups and disulfide bonds were determined according to the report described from Beveridge, Toma, and Nakai (1974) with few modifications. To determine the SH, 30 mg CPI samples were weighed and dissolved in 10 ml Tris-Gly buffer (0.086 M Tris, 0.09 Gly and 4 mM EDTA, pH = 8, denoted as Tris-Gly) containing 8 M urea. After that, 50 μl of Ellman’s reagent (5,5′-dithio-bis-2-nitrobenzoic acid in Tris-Gly buffer, 4 mg/ml) was added. The mixed dispersions were allowed to incubate in the dark at 25 °C for 60 min and then centrifuged at 8000 g for 5 min. The supernatants were collected and their absorbances at 412 nm were determined. Meanwhile the Tris-Gly buffer containing Ellman’s reagent was used as a blank. The contents of total SH were determined as follows: 15 mg CPI samples were dispersed in 10 ml Tris-Gly buffer containing 8 M urea, and 100 μl of 2-mercaptoethanol was subsequently added. These dispersions were then incubated at 25 °C for 60 min. After incubation, 10 ml of 12% trichloroacetic acid was added to the dispersion to precipitate the protein and centrifuged at 8000 g for 10 min. The precipitates were washed with 10 ml of 12% trichloroacetic acid three times and centrifuged to remove 2-mercaptoethanol. The precipitated proteins were redissolved in 10 ml Tris-Gly, and 50 μl Ellman’s reagent was added for colour development. The absorbance at 412 nm was determined. The content of SH was calculated as Eq. The ability of peanut flours and peanut protein concentrate to be functional is primarily due to their soluble protein contents. Proteins with high oil and water binding are desirable for use in meats, sausages, breads, and cakes while proteins with high emulsifying capacity are good for sausages, bologna, soups and salad dressing. Fermented peanut flour and the derived protein concentrate showed better functional properties, particularly, water holding and emulsifying capacity, than the unfermented flour and protein concentrate. Spray dried PPC developed from roasted peanut flour had better oil holding and emulsifying capacity than the flour itself and would be suitable for use in products like meats and sausage. The extremely high emulsifying capacity of this PPC makes it also a good candidate for food formulations requiring high emulsifying capacities such as salad dressing and creamy soup. The low viscosity of PPC suspension at room temperature and higher viscosity upon heating make PPC a desirable thickener for high protein soups. In addition, the fact that PPC with better functionality could be developed from roasted defatted peanut flour is an important advantage to the peanut oil industry because the roasted defatted peanut flour is an inexpensive by-product of peanut oil production. Thus, peanut protein isolates and concentrates have the potential to add value to the peanut industry and provide food processor with affordable source of plant proteins with unique flavor and functional characteristics.

WATER HOLDING CAPACITY (WHC):
The gel with good properties could fully capture and retain water in the three-dimensional crosslinked network structure ( Ainis et al., 2019 ). The WHC of PPI gels under different heat treatments is shown in Fig. 7 . The WHC of the PPI gels under the OH treatment was significantly higher than that under the CH treatment (86.73 g/100 g) ( P < 0.05). This might be due to the electric field effects that changed the charge distribution on the protein molecules and increased the intermolecular repulsion, thus promoting protein unfolding and improving the possibility of water binding ( Wang et al., 2020 ). Angel-Rendon, Filomena-Ambrosio, Cordon-Diaz, Benitez-Sastoque, and Sotelo-Diaz (2019) suggested that OH technology could quickly and uniformly process food, improving the large water loss caused by traditional methods. Under the condition of the same electric field strength or frequency, the WHC of PPI gels gradually increased with increasing frequency or decreasing electric field strength, but there was no significant difference among all samples ( P > 0.05). Increasing the electric field strength (from 5 V /cm to 20 V/cm) resulted in a 1.02% decrease (from 90.12 g/100 g to 89.07 g/100 g) in WHC at 50 Hz. The WHC of the OH 50 Hz 20 V/cm treatment reached the lowest value (89.07 g/100 g). This was attributed to less SH/S-S bonds exchange, resulting in less S S bonds cross-linking and lower protein aggregation. Therefore, the gel network could not maintain more moisture ( Wang et al., 2020 ).

TEXTURE PROFILE ANALYSIS (TPA):
The textural properties of the PPI gels under different heat treatments are shown in Table 2 . The CH-induced gel showed the highest hardness (286.59), gumminess (81.09), and chewiness (73.22). In this study, the hardness values of the OH-treated PPI gels were significantly lower than those of the control sample (P < 0.05). Gel hardness reflected WHC to some extent. The increase of WHC and the decrease of hardness of the gel treat with ohmic heating could be explained as OH gels have a finer structure and were less hard, so it is more conducive to water-protein interaction and can absorb and retain more water ( Rodrigues, Fasolin, et al., 2020 ). In addition, gel hardness increased significantly (P < 0.05) accompanied by the decrease of frequency (from 20 kHz to 50 Hz) and the increase of the electric field strength (from 5 V /cm to 20 V/cm). The increase in gumminess and chewiness was accompanied by the decrease in frequency and increase in electric field strength. The decrease in aggregate size and increase in soluble aggregates favored protein-protein cross-linking and the formation of a stronger gel network structure ( Li et al., 2020 ), thus enhancing gel hardness, gumminess, and chewiness. With the decrease of frequency (from 20 kHz to 50 Hz) and the increase of electric field strength (from 5 V/cm to 20 V/cm), the gel springiness decreased and then increased (from 0.90 to 0.88 to 0.90) and cohesiveness decreased (from 0.32 to 0.29). Overall, OH treatment affected the protein-protein interaction and then decreased the hardness, gumminess, and chewiness of the gel. Moreover, it changed the springiness and cohesiveness to varying degrees.

SCANNING ELECTRON MICROSCOPY (SEM):
SEM was used to observe the effects of the different heat treatments on the three-dimensional network structure of the gels. The SEM of the PPI gels under different heat treatments is shown in Fig. 8 . The structure of the CH-treated gel ( Fig. 8 a) was notably rough and bumpy, characterized by the large protein aggregates and poor WHC of the gel. This phenomenon was consistent with Peyrano, Lamballerie, Avanza, and Speroni (2021) , who studied heat-induced gelation of cowpea protein and found that the more uniform the gel network structure, the stronger WHC. In the traditional heating process, the existence of the hot surface meant that the heat was slow to transfer to the center of the sample, and the uneven heating for a long time resulted in the degradation of food quality. Compared with CH treatment, OH treatment changed the microstructure morphology of the PPI gel network to a more uniform, denser, and smooth one. This might be due to the decrease of free SH content in the protein after OH treatment to produce more intermolecular S S bonds, thus forming a uniform three-dimensional network structure. The OH 50 Hz-treated gel had a higher degree of cross-linking, smaller microstructural pores, and a smoother surface with a relatively uniform appearance. With the increase of electric field strength (from 5 V /cm to 20 V/cm) at OH 50 Hz, the microstructure of the gel became finer but not significantly ( Fig. 8 e, f, and g). Gelation was closely related to protein aggregates. Wu et al. (2019) found that when smaller aggregate size was involved in the subsequent gel formation, a more uniform and more cross-linked gel structure was formed. However, larger aggregates would weaken the gel network structure of the proteins ( Hua, Cui, Wang, Mine, & Poysa, 2005 ; Rodrigues, Fasolin, et al., 2020 ). With the increase of OH treatment frequency (from 50 Hz to 20 kHz), the aggregation degree of protein molecules increased, and the gel structure became irregular and less compact. Large irregular pores and uneven distribution were observed. Overall, the effect of the electric field on the gel microstructure was more significant at a lower frequency and higher electric field strength.

RHEOLOGICAL PROPERTIES:
The G' and G" could represent the elasticity and viscosity of the protein gel network structure. The rheological properties of the PPI gels under different heat treatments are shown in Fig. 9 a and b . Overall, all gel samples showed G' > G”, indicating that the elastic behavior was dominant in the samples, which confirmed the formation of the gel. In addition, G' and G“ treated with two different treatments showed a slight frequency dependence, indicating that the gels produced by both treatments all had weak gelation properties, which can be characterized as gel-like behavior. The G' and G" of the OH-treated samples were less than that of the CH-treated sample, and the viscoelasticity of the gel was weaker. This finding is consistent with the report by Rodrigues et al. (2015) . Gelation was related to the content of insoluble and soluble aggregates in the aggregate solution. Increasing the number of soluble aggregates would promote protein-protein cross-linking to obtain higher G' and G" values, while the existence of insoluble aggregates would hinder the formation of the three-dimensional network and reduce the degree of cross-linking ( Klost, Brzeski, & Drusch, 2020 ). The rheological properties of the gel were also related to the micro-network structure formed. The gel network structure with less coarseness showed higher elastic energy storage ability ( Munialo, Linden, & Jongh, 2014 ). Compared with the coarse gel obtained by OH treatment with high frequency or low field strength (20 kHz and 5 V /cm), the fine network structure formed at low frequency or high field strength (50 Hz and 20 V/cm) showed higher viscoelasticity. In addition, with increasing electric field strength (from 5 V/cm to 20 V/cm), there was great difference in viscoelasticity, even with no significant difference between the gel microstructure ( Fig. 8 e, f, and g).

Tartary buckwheat (Fagopyrum tataricum) is an important medicinal and edible plant
that is rich in bioactive substances such as protein, starch, and ﬂavonoids, and has a high
nutritional and medicinal value [1]. Tartary buckwheat protein (TBP) is the main bioactive
substance of Tartary buckwheat, accounting for approximately 15~17% of the whole seed.
It has a rich and balanced amino acid content and high nutritional value, and also has
a variety of biological activities, such as lowering blood pressure, lowering blood sugar,
and antioxidation [2–4]; as a high-quality natural plant protein, TBP has considerable
development prospects.

The physicochemical and functional properties of protein affect the process, nutrition,
and sensory elements of food to a great extent, and are important aspects to evaluate the
potential of proteins and provide guidance for their application. Recently, various methods
have been used to improve the structure and functional properties of proteins to achieve
the purpose of improving food quality. As a natural biological treatment technology,
germination has been widely used to improve the nutritional and processing characteristics
of plants. During plant germination, the endogenous protease is activated, the protein is
decomposed into amino acids and peptides [5], the protein molecular structure is unfolded,
the polypeptide chain is broken, and the water/oil binding site is exposed, which is
